Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "put together a clear prompt for a delivery summary for North Quay depot, but make it useful to the shift leads and not a general essay. the period is 1–30 April 2025, local depot dates. the intended reader is a lead who has to check what arrived and decide what to follow up, not a customer and not the finance team. summarize deliveries for this depot only. don't roll in other depots just because the same carrier serves them. The request is to help compare what was received during the month with the records, not to say that every delivery in the system was physically checked.

there are a few details on how the depot runs. North Quay has a morning receiving team and a late team; handover is at 14:30, and pallets waiting in the marked inspection lane can remain there across a shift change. A delivery logged after that handover can still belong to the same calendar day. show the date basis rather than assuming the late team means the next day. The intake board lists dock door, carrier, and receiving clerk, but those fields can be blank on older entries. don't treat a blank clerk name as proof that no one checked the load. The depot's delivery register is the working source for receipt status and units, while paper exception slips are used for damaged cartons and short shipments. Some slips are filed by the day they were written, not the day the truck arrived, so mention that limitation if it affects a comparison.

we need a readable account of received volume, plus anything the shift leads ought to inspect in the register or paper slips. The summary should distinguish received entries from entries still marked expected, held, or cancelled. Don't quietly combine those statuses. The data extract may not have a separate line for each carton, so describe units as recorded units and don't call them cartons unless a source says so. If a delivery has several rows, avoid claiming they are separate truck visits unless the source has a visit identifier. We have a monthly depot total in mind, but also want the daily pattern to be visible enough that a lead could spot a busy date or a gap. Don't invent a target, service-level threshold, or explanation for a rise or dip; none has been supplied.

please include the query below as supplied reference material in the prompt, intact. it is the query the analyst plans to use for a received-units-by-depot check. don't rewrite its filter, and don't imply that it has already been run or that its results are attached. The analyst says, “I want the receipt filter kept exactly as written, because expected loads should not be counted as received.”
SELECT depot_id, SUM(units) AS received_units
FROM deliveries
WHERE status = 'received' AND units > 9
GROUP BY depot_id;

there are some specific things to compare, not just a total. The lead wants the April received-units total, a day-by-day view for the depot, and a short note on which recorded deliveries or dates appear to need checking against the intake board or exception slips. Explain what evidence supports each flagged item, and keep an observed record separate from an inference. For example, a difference between the register and a slip can be described as a difference, but don't decide which source is right. Don't call a date a missed delivery just because its received count is zero; the available material doesn't establish what was scheduled. For dates with no matching received rows, say what the records show and leave the reason open. If the records don't let the analyst establish something, say that briefly instead of filling the gap.

The output constraint applies to the final written summary for the shift leads: make it exactly six numbered checklist items, numbered 1 through 6. Each item should be a compact paragraph, not a table, and the evidence or record reference must come before any suggested follow-up in that same item. Keep any suggested follow-up limited to checking a named source; don't recommend staffing, carrier penalties, or process changes. Item 1 should state the date range, depot, and basis of the summary; item 2 should cover the monthly received-units total; item 3 should give the daily pattern; items 4 and 5 should cover the record checks and evidence; item 6 should state relevant limitations and unresolved questions. Don't add a title, unnumbered introduction, extra bullets, or a conclusion after item 6. The six-item constraint is for the summary itself, not for this prompt or the query block.

For readability, use plain English and keep the wording direct. Use the depot name North Quay consistently, and make clear that the intended reader is the shift lead. Don't present an estimate as an exact count, and don't claim a total is verified against paper slips unless the comparison actually supports that. If the analyst later finds that a paper slip's arrival date differs from its filing date, the summary must identify which date was used and avoid treating the mismatch as a confirmed error. The shift supervisor told us, “A clean-looking number is not the same thing as a checked delivery.” Use that as a reminder of the audience's concern, not as a finding about April.

One more detail for the final item: the April register export may be incomplete for the last evening of the month because its refresh time is not confirmed. If the export does not show whether the late entries were included, say that the coverage is uncertain and ask for a refreshed export before treating the month as complete. If a refreshed export is not available, leave the coverage question unresolved; don't substitute an assumed cutoff or claim the last evening had no deliveries. Keep that condition in the prompt, since it changes what the analyst can say about the monthly total. The final summary should make no claim about deliveries outside North Quay or dates outside April, and it should not turn the query into a result. End the prompt by retaining the instruction to keep the final section, item 6, complete, including the refresh-time condition and any unresolved coverage question.", "output": "Write a clear, direct summary of deliveries for the shift leads at North Quay depot for 1–30 April 2025, using local depot dates.
